notes.meaning: Moses spoke the Lord's instructions directly to the leaders of the tribes of Israel. These leaders had the duty to teach the laws to the people and make sure they were properly obeyed. God guided the entire nation by working through recognized leaders.

other.label: Modern scholarship
other.view: Some scholars view the mention of tribal leaders here as a sign that this law came from a distinct source or was placed in the text by a different editor than the surrounding chapters.

notes.meaning: When a man makes a solemn vow or takes an oath to go without something, he must keep his word. A vow is a voluntary promise made to God, but once spoken aloud, it becomes a serious duty. Breaking that promise means treating one's own word and faith as worthless.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Catholic teaching points to these rules on vows to support religious vows, including lifelong pledges of poverty, chastity, and obedience in monastic orders.

notes.meaning: This rule concerns a young woman who still lives at home under the care of her father. Because she was dependent on her family, her choices had a direct effect on the whole household. Even so, she was free to show personal faith by making vows directly to the Lord.

If the father hears about his daughter's promise and says nothing to stop her, his silence counts as consent. Since he did not object, her vow remains fully in force. She is then required to carry out everything she pledged.

If her father forbids the vow on the very day he hears of it, her promise is completely cancelled. The Lord absolves her, which means he forgives her and releases her from any duty to pay the vow. God respects parental authority and does not blame a daughter when her father overrules her.

This situation looks at a woman who gets married while still carrying an unfulfilled vow from her youth. She might have entered a pledge carefully or spoken rashly without thinking. When she enters marriage, oversight of her promises shifts to her new husband.

If her new husband learns about her prior pledge and raises no objection that day, the promise stands. By keeping quiet, he agrees that she should fulfill her obligation. Her vow remains fully binding before the Lord.

If her husband objects on the day he learns about her vow, he can cancel it immediately. This protected the new home from taking on unexpected burdens. Because she honors her husband's decision, God pardons her and releases her from the pledge.

A widow or a divorced woman answers directly to God for her promises. Because she is not under the authority of a husband or father, no man can cancel her vows. Whatever pledge she makes to the Lord must be carried out in full.

This case deals with a woman who makes a vow while living in her husband's house. Her pledge might involve offering a sacrifice or denying herself certain pleasures. Because her actions affect the joint household, her husband has a say in the matter.

When a husband hears his wife's vow and says nothing against it, his silence gives full permission. Every pledge and obligation she took upon herself must be kept. She is bound to perform what she promised to the Lord.

If the husband cancels her vows on the day he hears them, none of her promises remain binding. His spoken objection removes the obligation entirely. God forgives her for leaving the vow unpaid because her husband set it aside.

A husband has the right to confirm or void any promise his wife makes, including pledges to deny herself through fasting. Such personal vows could harm her health or strain the marriage relationship. God gave the husband authority to protect family health and peace.

A husband cannot wait indefinitely to make up his mind. If days go by and he says nothing, his silence legally confirms her vows. Once he allows the vow to stand by his silence, he loses the right to cancel it later.

If a husband consents by silence at first but later tries to stop his wife from keeping her vow, God holds him guilty. The fault belongs to him for delaying his response and causing the broken promise. The wife is released from blame, and the husband bears the penalty for the sin.

These rules summarize God's laws concerning vows made by wives and young daughters. The Lord set up these instructions to balance personal devotion to God with peace and order in the home. They remind believers that honoring God also includes respecting the duties of family life.
